title: U.S. captures third women's world hockey title in 4 years, downing rival Canadians
summary: Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek each scored twice as the United States defended its women's world hockey title with a 6-2 win over Canada in Monday's gold-medal game in Herning, Denmark.

image.caption: Hilary Knight of the United States scores one of her two goals in Monday's 5-2 gold-medal victory over Canada in Herning, Denmark. (Ida Marie Odgaard/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)

blocks.text: Hockey·Recap
Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek each scored twice as the United States defended its women's world hockey title with a 6-2 win over Canada in Monday's gold-medal game in Herning, Denmark.
2026 Olympic champions Knight, Panneck score twice; Sweden earns bronze in Denmark
Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek each scored twice as the United States defended its women's world hockey title with a 6-2 win over Canada in Monday's gold-medal game.

Knight, the 37-year-old American captain who won her 11th gold medal in her 16th world championship, added an assist. She finished the tournament with a personal-best nine goals and now has 76 world-championship goals in her career.

"I love scoring goals. I love playing with this group, playing with great players, it's a lot of fun," Knight said. "The game's super fast, but it's best on best and I love finding that challenge and finding it back in the net," Knight said.

Lacey Eden and Hayley Scamurra also scored for the Americans, who won their third straight gold-medal game over their archrivals. The U.S. also beat Canada in the final of the 2025 world championship and the 2026 Winter Olympics.

"It hurts," said Canada co-captain Renata Fast. "Not the result that we were looking for and the game got away from us a little bit, but there were moments that our team really took it to them and had some good looks, good opportunities."
Captain Hilary Knight guides Americans to a 2nd-straight women's world championship title

American defender Caroline Harvey picked up an assist to finish with a tournament-leading 16 points (six goals, 10 assists) and was named tournament MVP. U.S. forward Taylor Fox added her 13th assist, setting a tournament record. Aerin Frankel made 18 saves.
Sarah Fillier scored twice for Canada, which failed to build on its tournament-best 13 gold medals. The Americans are now just behind with 12 gold. Ann-Renee Desbiens stopped 21 shots.
Canada had won three of four world women's tournaments before the back-to-back U.S. wins.
"I thought we came out pretty hard, first period, second period, but it's the small details, small habits that winning a gold medal comes down to," Fillier said.

items: Canada tops Sweden, advancing to gold-medal game against U.S.
New-look Canadian team has an eye on the future

blocks.text: Canada came to Denmark with a young squad that was missing some experienced veterans, most notably Maire-Philip Poulin. Canada's talismanic captain is out of action while recovering from knee surgery.

"We have been together for 25 days here, and these are the first 25 days that this group has been together," Fast said. "This is the start of building our team with a lot of new faces, a fresh group. We have a lot to be proud about; we came together really well off the ice and we are finding our chemistry on the ice. The group we have in the locker room are really quality people."
Canada opened the scoring at 11:03 of the first period as Fillier slid the puck under Frankel to extend her goal-scoring streak to five games.
Fillier's goal put the U.S. behind for the first time at the tournament, but it didn't last long.

The Americans tied it at 16:17 of the first period after sustained pressure. Knight picked up the rebound of a Tessa Janecke shot and beat Desbiens for her eighth goal of the tournament and 75th career world championship goal.
U.S. converts 2-on-1 for go-ahead goal

Pannek put the Americans ahead at 11:33 of the second period, beating Desbiens on a two-on-one after Scamurra carried the puck from the U.S. blueline and slid a pass past sprawling Canadian defender Sophie Jaques.
Knight scored her second of the game on a power play at 17:51 of the second, taking a pass in the slot from Megan Keller and beating Desbiens.

Pannek, the leading scorer in the Professional Women's Hockey League in 2025, scored her second of the game and fifth of the tournament 1:29 into the third period when she tipped a knuckling puck past Desbiens. Eden made it 5-1 with a goal just 1:19 later.

blocks.text: Fillier, who missed Canada's first two games in Denmark with an injury sustained in a pre-tournament game against the U.S., scored her sixth goal of the tournament at 3:28 of the third when she collected the puck at the U.S. blueline and wired a shot past Frankel.
"Playing Canada, it's always a battle, back and forth the whole 60 minutes," Harvey said. "We knew it was gonna be a challenge, we knew what to expect, and they deserve a lot of credit."
"It was a hard fought battle, but we were ready for it," she added.

Canada pulled Desbiens in favour of an extra attacker with just under five minutes left in the game, but Scamurra forced a turnover in the American zone and chipped the puck into the empty Canadian net at 16:33 of the third.
Bronze game: Sweden 2, Finland 1

Earlier Monday, Hilda Svensson scored the decisive shootout goal and Sweden medalled at the women’s world hockey championship for the first time since 2007 by defeating Finland 2-1 in the bronze medal final.

Sweden rallied from a 1-0 deficit with Lina Ljungblom tying the score with a power-play goal from the slot with six minutes left in regulation. Svensson, a 20-year-old sophomore at Ohio State, had an assist on Ljungblom’s goal.

Svensson then scored Sweden’s second shootout goal by driving in from the right wing and beating Sanni Ahola with a snapshot inside the far post. Ebba Svensson Traff sealed the win by stopping Finland’s final two attempts, including a right pad save on Emmi Juusela.

Sweden rallied from a 1-0 deficit to beat Finland for the bronze medal at the women's world hockey championship on Monday in Herning, Denmark. Lina Ljungblom and Hilda Svensson, in the shootout, had the goals. (Ida Marie Odgaard/Ritzau Scanpix/AFP via Getty Images)
Svensson Traff stopped 29 shots through overtime and four of five shootout attempts.

Michelle Karvinen opened the scoring with a power-play goal with 3:05 left in the second period, and Noora Tulus scored Finland’s lone shootout goal. The 36-year-old Karvinen's goal was her team career record 27th in world championship play, moving her one ahead of Petra Nieminen.
Ahola finished with 35 saves through overtime and allowed a shootout goal by Tilde Grillfors.
Sweden was making its first tournament medal-game appearance since a 4-1 loss to Finland in 2009. Sweden won its third medal after also winning bronze in 2005.
The Swedes were coming off a promising fourth-place finish at the Milano-Cortina Olympics in February in which they lost the bronze-medal final to Switzerland.
With files from The Associated Press
